item.title: A flexible new route to designer materials built from nanoparticles
item.description: Pliable connector molecules could be key to creating nanoparticle-based materials for photonics, chemical catalysis, medicine, and more.
item.dc:creator: Zach Winn | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Creating better-performing materials comes down to having more control over their structure at the smallest possible scale. One particularly effective way to accomplish that is using nanoparticles, which have highly customizable shapes and sizes and have already shown promise in applications across energy, medicine, and electronics.

But the process of turning nanoparticles into useful new materials has been hampered by the difficulty of controlling the number and direction of the links between each particle and its neighbors. Researchers have tried changing the shape of particles or precisely aligning the rigid connector chains between them, but both of those methods limit the material structures nanoparticles are able to form and are difficult to scale.

A team including researchers from MIT is taking a different approach. The researchers developed a tunable way to use super-flexible connector molecules that regulate the packing of nanoparticle networks by intentionally deforming based on their surrounding environment. In a paper published today in Nature Materials, the researchers showed how connector flexibility and electric charges can be used to tune the network’s structure, and they used the technique to create new kinds of nanoparticle-based materials.

The approach could offer a more versatile way to create high-performing materials for photonics, chemical catalysis, medicine, agriculture, and more.

“People are interested in nanoparticle superlattices because of the promise of building designer materials where you have more say in what types of structures they can actually build into,” says Rob Macfarlane, the Richard P. Simmons (1953) Professor in Metallurgy in MIT’s Department of Materials Science and Engineering. “This is a new approach in nanoparticle assembly that hasn’t been investigated before. It’s exciting to have a new tool that is so counterintuitive. It’s the exact opposite of what the dogma has been for 20 years: that you need to make connector ligands rigid, and any deviation causes assembly to fail. We showed if you just crank it all the way to the opposite extreme, it works just as well.”

Joining Macfarlane on the paper are MIT PhD candidate Nicholas Sbalbi; University of Delaware doctoral student Stephen Kronenberger; MIT undergraduate Hana Shinzawa; Matthew Ye PhD ’26; and former University of Delaware professor Arthi Jayaraman.

More flexible structures

A foundational truth in materials science is that a material’s structure governs its function.

“That means if you know what your building blocks are and how they’re arranged, you can explain what properties materials have,” Macfarlane says. “Controlling that is how you make materials that have new properties.”

Nanoparticles give scientists a flexible building block to make materials with desired properties, and individual nanoparticles are already used in applications as diverse as drug delivery, energy storage, computing, and sensing. But assembling them into larger structures has proven to be a challenge because of how tightly they tend to pack together.

To overcome that challenge, researchers make nanoparticles different shapes, which changes how they connect. They can also make only specific parts of the particles’ surfaces sticky so they form different patterns.

“The challenge with both of those approaches is they’re difficult to do synthetically as we make the particles,” Macfarlane explains. “The methods for defining stickiness that have been developed are always bespoke: They work for one material, at one size scale, in one condition. It’s good for studying, but you can’t do much with it.”

Both methods also require connector molecules, called ligands, at the surface of the nanoparticles to be rigid so they stay at the specific angles needed to maintain the formation researchers want, which further limits their functionality.

For their new study, the researchers wanted to turn that approach on its head.

“We thought, ‘Let’s do the exact opposite: make the bonds so flexible it doesn’t matter what direction they’re initially pointing.’ The ligands can then reorganize as the particles come together, and that reorganization itself limits how many neighbors each particle can bind,” Macfarlane says.

Macfarlane’s group has spent years creating ways to make different kinds of particles from grafts of polymers. The nanoparticles in their new system have flexible ligands with electrically charged tips, some positively charged and others negatively charged. The opposites attract, so the ligands bend to connect with opposite charges.

“The idea is, instead of defining a specific direction the bonds are going to occur in with complicated synthesis methods, we just said, ‘The bonds are going to be as flexible as they want to be, and they’ll spontaneously go to whatever valency is going to maximize bond stability,’” Macfarlane says.

In experiments led by Sbalbi, the researchers showed they could control the connections by changing the nanoparticle sizes and ligand chain lengths. They also used the technique to assemble the nanoparticles into previously unseen crystal structures.

“Without having to predesign where the particles connect or what their shapes are, we can control the number of bonds each particle has,” Macfarlane explains. “The amount of flexibility of the polymer dictates how many bonds it has. It allows us to lower the number of bonds each particle has and make lattices we have never seen before.”

A new path toward customizable materials

Macfarlane believes the system is a step toward getting custom nanoparticle-based materials out of the research lab and into the world.

“We in the nanoparticle assembly community talk about having completely independent control over what your particle is and what assembly it goes into,” Macfarlane says. “In theory, that should be the case. In reality, it absolutely has not been.”

More broadly, the researchers say their approach establishes ligand flexibility as a new path to making material structures that can be customized at scale.

“Nanoparticle superlattices offer a way to create designer materials where your building blocks have all sort sorts of unique properties,” Macfarlane says. “But just densely packing these nanoparticles together limits your applications. This offers a way to get less dense formations of nanoparticles, and that’s where a lot of the interesting applications are.”

The work was supported, in part, by the National Science Foundation, the Department of Energy, the U.S. Army and the U.S. Navy.

item.title: MIT engineers design a safer, more efficient vaccination system for farmed fish
item.description: Water-resistant microneedles made from food-grade silk could deliver vaccines to help prevent the spread of disease in aquaculture.
item.dc:creator: Zach Winn | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Fish that are cultivated in pools or ponds are an increasingly important source of food around the world. Unfortunately, disease outbreaks can cause substantial losses in aquaculture. 

Fish farmers use vaccines to prevent disease outbreaks just like regular farmers, but vaccinating a fish is a lot harder than vaccinating a cow. The most effective way to vaccinate fish today uses needles, but there are several downsides to this process, both for the fish and the farmers. 

Now a team of researchers at MIT and the U.S. Department of Agriculture has developed a potentially better way to deliver vaccines. The approach uses water-resistant, food-grade microneedles that can lightly penetrate and remain attached to fish skin before decomposing. In a new paper published in ACS Nano, the researchers described their system and showed it could be used to deliver a range of cargos, such as bacterial vaccines.

“To feed the world we need more fish, which are a major source of protein and nutrition,” says Benedetto Marelli, a professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “Aquaculture is a very effective way of producing a large amount of fish. Our approach could give farmers a more precise tool to maintain fish health. Farmers are really concerned about the health care of these fish, so providing them with better tools is really important.”

Joining Marelli on the paper are Meng Li, an MIT postdoc and first author on the paper; Jad Raad MEng ’24; Yunteng Cao PhD ’22, a postdoc at Yale University; Yue Hu, a former MIT postdoc; Colleen Wolfe MEng ’23; Doyoon Kim, a former MIT postdoc; Bradley Frank, a current MIT postdoc; and Gregory Wiens, a researcher at the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s National Center for Cool and Cold Water Aquaculture.

Better vaccine delivery

Aquaculture holds enormous potential to address food insecurity, reduce energy consumption, and decarbonize global food systems. In 2021, for the first time, farmed aquatic animals exceeded wild-caught aquatic animals in global food production by weight.

“The world’s population is going to grow by almost 2 billion people by 2050,” Marelli says. “Fish provide access to essential nutrition. They are high in protein and healthy fat, which are difficult to make, so the world is trying to produce more fish. But there are many challenges associated with fisheries.”

To prevent losses to disease, farmers use a range of automated and manual vaccination strategies, each with their own drawbacks. Some treatments can go into fish food, but those might not reach every fish. Another method is putting the treatment directly in a pool and immersing the fish in the treated water. That approach requires far higher quantities of treatment and, again, isn’t 100 percent effective.

The most effective way to vaccinate fish is with metal needles. The process requires farmers to sedate the fish, then get them out of the water and onto a conveyor belt, where workers hurry to vaccinate the fish and get them back in the water to minimize harm.

“Workers inject fish one by one,” Li explains. “It’s high intensity, there’s a risk of cross contamination of blood-borne diseases, and workers may accidentally jab themselves because they are working so quickly. So it’s labor intensive, costly, stressful for fish, and dangerous for workers.”

Marelli’s lab has been developing silk microneedles to deliver nutrients to plants for years. The silk has been classified as safe for human consumption in food coatings and can degrade in the body or in the environment over time.

A few years ago, Marelli learned about the challenges with vaccinating fish at a conference in Southeast Asia, where aquaculture is an especially important part of the aquatic food supply. His lab received support from the Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS) to explore adapting the silk platform he’d developed for underwater use for fish. But the early silk designs would quickly dissolve when exposed to water, releasing the vaccine immediately and failing to penetrate fish skin.

Li, a biomedical engineer, started to work on the project in Marelli’s lab beginning in 2022. In 2024, she received a fellowship from the USDA, which provided funding as well as important connections with collaborators at the agency and beyond. For example, the U.S. Geological Survey gave the researchers access to a DNA vaccine for rainbow trout.

Marelli credits Li with finding a way around silk’s tendency to soften when exposed to water. The system described in the new paper uses a thin layer of shellac, an insect-secreted resin used in food coating and pills, to make silk microneedles water-resistant by providing a moisture barrier that remains intact before fish injection.

“The material choice is critical because we’re dealing with food, even though we expect the microneedle to fall out of the fish or to be degraded in their body,” Li says. “Our criteria were safety for fish and humans alike.”

The researchers showed the microneedles can store a range of vaccines, and they demonstrated different versions of the microneedles that lasted longer in the water or diffused vaccines more quickly.

“In some cases, you may want the vaccine released within 15 minutes, but in others, the release can last 10 or even 24 hours,” Li says. “That could be better for other therapeutic uses beyond vaccines.”

The microneedles were also able to preserve half of the DNA plasmids’ structure when stored for four weeks in dry conditions.

“That stability is important, particularly for the last mile of delivery, because aquaculture is mostly done in rural areas,” Marelli says. “This allows farmers to not need to rely on the infrastructure to maintain the cold chain.”

Protecting fish

Just like terrestrial animal vaccines, fish vaccines are most effective when administered early in life before disease exposure. That means the fish that farmers want to inject are small, further complicating vaccination. The researchers believe their approach could offer a better way to vaccinate small fish, and they tested it in rainbow trout.

“In trout aquaculture, one of the biggest challenges we face is preventing disease early in a fish’s life, because traditional needle‑based vaccination just doesn’t work well until the fish reach about 30 grams, which leaves the smallest juveniles unprotected during a critical growth period,” says Wiens. “What our research shows is food‑grade silk fibroin microneedles can deliver vaccines underwater to fish as small as 1 to 2 grams. We designed these single‑use microneedles to pierce wet skin, stay attached while the fish swim, and release either bacterin or DNA vaccines in a controlled way.”

The researchers say there is still work to be done before their device can be seamlessly used at scale in fish farms. But they believe this paper is an important first step.

“We have all the components to believe this technology could be developed further,” Marelli says. “There are so many challenges with aquaculture and fish vaccination right now. We need to support farmers to operate safely, improve working conditions, protect their business, make vaccination more accessible, and improve the living conditions of farmed fish and ultimately the quality of the food we eat. This new technology could be a much more effective and safer approach.”

The work was supported, in part, by MIT’s Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab and the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

item.title: Study pinpoints states with steepest warming trends since 1980
item.description: The findings indicate where adaptive measures are needed most around the United States.
item.dc:creator: Mark Dwortzan | Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy
item.content:encoded:
Global warming, the observed increase in the Earth’s average global surface temperature since preindustrial (1850-1900) times, currently stands at around 1.63 degrees Celsius. While this number is expected to continue to rise, local temperatures will not go up uniformly around the world. In regions where warming trends are most pronounced, local adaptation and resilience measures will be especially critical to minimizing risks to ecosystems, agricultural productivity, the built environment, human health, and economic well-being. 

To that end, a new open-access study in the journal Scientific Data identifies the highest-risk regions for warming within the United States. Using data from well-known, high-resolution climate and weather datasets (MERRA2 and ERA5) covering the years 1980-2022, researchers at the MIT Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3) report global warming-attributed trends in monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature for every U.S. state. 

The study finds that Alaska, Utah, New Mexico, Colorado, and Nevada have experienced the strongest average warming trends; the lowest occurred in Hawaii, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Arkansas. Across the country, warming trends were most pronounced during the summer and fall, particularly in September and November. Alaska has the highest historical maximum daily temperature warming (an average of 2.5 C of monthly-averaged maximum daily temperature increase per degree of global warming), while Hawaii has the lowest average historical warming, at 0.8 C. 

The authors expect that barring unforeseen local anomalies, these state-by-state temperature trends will continue unabated as ongoing global emissions from human activities continue to raise the average global temperature.

“Based on these results, we encourage decision-makers to assess states that have undergone the steepest increases in maximum and minimum daily temperatures, and identify where continued trends would indicate a rapid progression toward thresholds beyond which natural and managed resources, ecosystems, and infrastructure can function safely,” says MIT CS3 Deputy Director C. Adam Schlosser, a co-author of the study. “In such cases, triaging and adaptive measures would take a high priority. By directing resources to where they are needed most, state and regional planners could significantly reduce climate-related physical and financial risks.”

Unlike previous efforts to report temperature trends across the United States, this study aggregates average maximum, minimum, and mean daily temperature data at the state level for each month of the year, providing actionable information for planners in government, industry, and civil society.

item.title: Q&A: Hey AI, who should I vote for this year?
item.description: MIT professors Adam Berinsky and Chara Podimata discuss a new project to track how AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Abby Abazorius | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
People are peppering artificial intelligence chatbots everyday with questions, but when it comes to politics and the looming 2026 U.S. midterm elections, what role are AI platforms playing? Could an AI chatbot sway a voter to switch parties or re-examine their political beliefs? 

MIT researchers have built a new dashboard, called the LLM Election Observatory, to examine, in real-time, how popular AI chatbots are responding to questions about the 2026 midterm elections. The team behind the dashboard — led by Professor Adam Berinsky, Assistant Professor Chara Podimata, and Professor Charles Stewart III — has extensive experience studying voting and election administration, AI and misinformation, and how AI systems are impacting human decision making. In an effort to better understand how AI is shaping the election, they designed the dashboard to simulate how individuals across the country communicate with chatbots. 

The team tracks how different AI systems respond to the same fixed set of questions on a range of topics, including election certification, hot-button issues, result predictions, news coverage, and more. Every few days, the LLM Election Observatory team runs the questions through the chatbots again, monitoring how their responses vary as the election gets closer depending on user location, political party affiliation, identity and other factors. The goal of this work is not to merely understand how AI systems spread information, but also better comprehend how they are shaping political discourse and voter understanding of political issues across the country. 

MIT News chatted with Podimata, the Class of 1942 Career Development Professor, an assistant professor of operations research and statistics in the MIT Sloan School of Management, and a member of the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems; and Berinsky, the Mitsui Professor and a professor in the Department of Political Science, about their work with the LLM Election Observatory, how AI could impact the midterms, and what voters should keep in mind when they interact with chatbots.

Q: What was the inspiration for this project and what are you hoping to learn through the LLM Election Observatory?

Podimata: People are increasingly using AI chatbots to find and make sense of political and election-related information. That makes it important to understand what information these systems actually provide, not just at one moment in time but throughout an election cycle. This is particularly challenging because the models themselves are continually getting updates, the political information inputs available to them are themselves changing, and their answers can depend on how a user asks a question or what information the user provides about themselves.

One basic problem is that we currently do not have a good historical record of this information environment. If an AI system gives a particular answer about an election today and gives a different answer several weeks later, it can be very difficult to reconstruct after the fact what voters would have seen at each point in time. One important goal of our project is simply to systematically document that environment as it develops and make the resulting data available to other researchers and to the public.

Ultimately, factual accuracy is only the first frontier. We absolutely need to understand whether chatbots provide accurate political information, but we also need to pay just as much attention to the subtler ways in which they may shape people’s understanding of political issues. Differences in framing, emphasis, uncertainty, and cited sources can matter enormously, even in the absence of outright misinformation.  

Q: Professor Podimata, you studied how LLMs shaped political discourse and information during the 2024 election. What were the main takeaways of that research and how did those findings inform this new project?

Podimata: The LLM Election Observatory builds on my previous work during the 2024 presidential election, which found evidence of meaningful variation in AI models’ responses over time and across prompt framings, as well as differences in how models characterized candidates and implicitly anticipated the election outcome. 

The 2026 midterms give us an opportunity to expand that work substantially. Midterm elections are particularly interesting because there are many state and local contests unfolding simultaneously, alongside broader national political narratives. Our new audit survey therefore asks both contest-specific questions about the U.S. House and Senate candidates, but also broader questions about voting information and other aspects of the election information environment.

Q: Why do you think it’s so important to be studying how chatbots are responding to political queries across different groups of users?

Podimata: We all build our own “microcosms” through our interactions with chatbots. And yet, we lack systematic ways of understanding how these individualized information environments are shaped by who we are or how they evolve over time as we and the information environment changes. 

For example, people may not realize that what their favorite chatbot tells them about a political issue may be quite different from what their friend’s favorite chatbot tells them about the exact same issue. And importantly, these differences matter even when the information being provided is factually correct. Chatbots may frame the same facts differently, emphasize different aspects of an issue, express different levels of uncertainty, or draw on entirely different sources, even when responding to identical queries between different users. As a result, two users may walk away with very different perceptions of the same underlying facts, without ever realizing that their experiences differed. 

In some ways, this brings back many of the concerns we (as researchers and society) have grappled with in the context of social media. On social media, users and researchers could, at least to some extent, observe the information circulating across different Facebook groups, Instagram accounts, or TikTok communities. With chatbots, these information environments are largely invisible to anyone outside the individual conversation. We cannot easily observe what different users are being told, let alone systematically compare those responses or track how they change over time. This is precisely why projects like the LLM Election Observatory are so important: By systematically collecting and publicly sharing chatbot responses, we can begin to make these otherwise invisible differences observable and open to scrutiny.

Q: What sorts of questions and AI responses are you tracking through the dashboard?

Podimata: There are several questions we ultimately want this dataset to help us study. For example: Do different models provide systematically different information for the same questions? Do their responses change over the course of the campaign? Does the answer a particular model gives change depending on how a user frames the question or describes themselves (e.g., does it change if the model gets informed that the user is a Democrat or a Republican)? And, finally, what are the sources that the models pull information from when answering election-related questions? 

Our public dashboard is an important part of the project. We want people both from and outside of academia to be able to see the data we are collecting as the election unfolds rather than only seeing the results months later in an academic paper. The dashboard therefore presents the underlying data and some preliminary descriptive analyses, and we plan to make the dataset available for other researchers to study as well. We expect the dashboard to evolve as the data and our methods evolve.

Through this dashboard, we wanted to build on the scientific methodology we developed in 2024 but also to make the research much more accessible and useful to the public while the election is actually unfolding. Not only that, but the addition of MIT political science experts in the team cannot be overstated; Adam and Charles have really helped expand the questions that we are asking in our audit.

Q: What do you wish voters across the country knew about AI chatbots when it comes to searching for election information?

Berinsky: People should be sure to remember that just because a chatbot sounds confident doesn’t mean it is accurate. AI systems are designed to answer the questions that people ask them in an authoritative voice even when they are wrong, incomplete, or leaning on a weak source. These answers are a reasonable place to start, but voters shouldn’t stop there.

Q: What are your findings thus far?

Podimata: We have not yet done the full, longitudinal analysis, so we are only going to talk about broad strokes here, but a few broad patterns seem to be visible in the 2026 data. Across the different user identities we present, we see differences in how the answers are presented, in which sources a model cites, and in tone — sometimes even when the underlying facts are the same. What we cannot yet say is how stable those differences are, how they move over the course of the election, or how a real person would read and react to them. Our future analyses will take this up. It also underscores why the continuous record of responses we are collecting matters more than any single snapshot that you might see in the days around the election.

Q: Professor Berinsky, your research has also shown that in some cases AI chatbots can be harnessed to help refute misinformation. Can you talk a bit about this?

Berinsky: In my undergraduate course on information and social media I have been talking for a while about how AI can cut both ways. On one hand, these tools can generate misleading claims in text, pictures, and video at a scale we have never seen. Basically, AI can help bad actors “flood the zone” with misinformation. On the other hand, some of the most promising recent work demonstrates that evidence-based dialogues with a chatbot can durably reduce belief in conspiracy theories and other beliefs that are not supported by the balance of publicly available evidence. 

AI has the potential to do such debunking at scale — something we have long struggled to do. The lesson from decades of misinformation research is that any technology (be it print, radio, or television in earlier eras) is not inherently good or bad for promoting truth. The devil is in the details in how it is built and deployed. Independent auditing like this project can help us assess the ultimate impact of such technologies.

Q: Can you talk a bit about your overall goal with this research? 

Podimata: AI is a transformative technology, and people understandably have very different expectations (and feelings) about what it will mean for society at large. All of us have people in our lives that are overly enthusiastic about AI, others that are deeply concerned, and many more that are somewhere in between trying to understand what this technology can and cannot do. Our goal here is not to begin from the assumption that AI is either good or bad for elections. Instead, we hope to shed some light onto one part of this transformation: what information major AI systems are actually giving people about an election as it unfolds.

item.title: MIT engineers create nanoparticles for delivering personalized cancer vaccines
item.description: The particles carry a customized dose of cancer antigens that can provoke a strong immune response against tumors.
item.dc:creator: Anne Trafton | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
A nanoscale particle with a unique structure, developed at MIT, holds potential as a customizable delivery vehicle for personalized cancer vaccines.

The backbone of the vaccine is a modified, harmless bacteriophage called M13, which forms a nanofiber that can be coated with cancer antigens. By precisely controlling the density of those cancer proteins, the researchers found that they could create a vaccine that prevents the development of colon tumors in mice.

This type of delivery particle could be adapted to carry many different antigens, allowing for the creation of personalized vaccines to treat individual patients’ tumors, the researchers say.

“The great thing about this is that it’s modular and we could switch out different antigens on demand, so you could design it to be patient-specific and target a known antigen for a particular kind of cancer,” says Angela Belcher, the James Mason Crafts Professor of Biological Engineering and Materials Science and Engineering and a member of the Koch Institute.

Belcher is the senior author of the study, which appears today in the journal Advanced Healthcare Materials. Shengnan Huang, research scientist at the Koch Institute, is the paper’s lead author. Jack Rudrum, Huaiyao Peng, and Hao Nghi Luu, graduate students at the Koch Institute, are also authors of the paper.

Viral vaccine assembly

For more than 20 years, Belcher’s lab has been deploying the M13 bacteriophage in a variety of applications. This virus, which is harmless to humans, consists of a single strand of DNA coated in a protein shell, or capsid. 

Belcher has previously developed techniques for generating materials by engineering these viruses to self-assemble into nanoscale scaffolds. By coating these scaffolds with inorganic materials, they can create functional devices such as batteries, semiconductors, solar cells, and catalysts, with precise control over the electronic, optical, and magnetic properties of the materials.

More recently, Belcher’s lab has been developing methods to control features of the phage that could allow it to be repurposed for medical applications, including vaccine delivery. 

“We’re taking this toolkit that we’ve worked on and developed over decades and formatting it to be specific for vaccine therapeutics,” Belcher says. “Some of the lessons learned from making batteries and all these other things are now being fine-tuned to make personalized vaccines.”

The capsid that surrounds the M13 phage forms a long filament made from viral proteins. To create vaccines, the researchers modify one of these proteins, known as pVIII, by attaching an antigen to the end of the protein. This can be done by adding the gene for the antigen to the virus’s DNA.

Some of the lab’s previous work had suggested that changing the density of cancer antigens attached to the capsid could affect the strength of the resulting immune response. In the new study, Huang wanted to find a way to control that density. 

“The antigen is the specific target we want to initiate the immune response against, which means we have to ensure the right dose of antigen to make sure that we can have a strong immune response,” she says.

Huang discovered that she could increase the density of the modified pVIII proteins by adding one or two negatively charged amino acids to the protein sequence. The density could be further fine-tuned by adding a genetic mutation that slows down production of the antigen protein.

In this study, the researchers also figured out how to boost the phage’s own ability to act as a vaccine adjuvant, by changing the genetic sequence of the virus’s DNA. Most vaccines need to be delivered along with an adjuvant such as aluminum hydroxide, which helps to stimulate a strong immune response. However, the M13 phage can act as an adjuvant itself because single-stranded DNA activates a pathway called TLR9, which is part of the body’s innate immune system.

“We can control the exact length. We can control the exact antigen expression, density, pattern, the exact adjuvant amount. A lot of times with a vaccine, you’ll have to put a different adjuvant with it, but now it’s all genetically encoded,” Belcher says. 

Targeting tumors

Using these techniques, the researchers showed that they could design phages that express an antigen called SIINFEKL at densities ranging from 6 percent to 70 percent. SIINFEKL, a small protein that can be engineered into tumors, is often used as a model to test vaccine effectiveness.

The researchers tested two of these vaccines in mice, one with 6 percent density and one with 35 percent, and found that the one with 35 percent was the most protective. 

After vaccination with the higher-density particles, mice were much less likely to develop tumors when later exposed to melanoma cancer cells expressing the SIINFEKL antigen. These mice also generated more T cells targeting SIINFEKL. This is, in part, because dendritic cells, which help to activate T cells, were more likely to take up vaccines with higher antigen density, the researchers found.

In another set of experiments, the researchers created and tested a vaccine carrying a neoantigen, which is only present in the tumor cells. This protein, known as ADPGK, is specifically expressed by colon tumors in a mouse model of cancer. When given the higher density vaccine, these mice were much less likely to develop colon tumors.

In this study, the researchers tested the vaccine as a way to prevent cancer from developing, and in their previous work, they adapted it for use to treat mouse colon tumors that have already formed. In the future, they also hope to use it to combat other types of cancer.

“This interesting work adds another cog to improve the translational potential of the M13 phage platform for cancer immunotherapeutics,” says Alberto Danielli, an associate professor of molecular biology at the University of Bologna, who was not involved in the study. “I look forward to seeing whether this platform is also effective against established tumors and whether additional tumor antigens can be displayed with comparable molecular and immunological efficacy.”

This platform could be especially well-suited for personalized cancer vaccines, because many different antigens could be swapped into the vaccine.

“Because this is a modularly engineered platform, we can change the antigen we are interested in. For colon cancer, we use this specific antigen. For other types of cancer, we can just plug in other antigens and they can be assembled in this platform,” Huang says.

The research was funded, in part, by the Koch Institute Frontier Research Program, the Marble Center for Cancer Nanomedicine, and the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency.

item.title: Magnetic sensors track muscle movement, for better prosthetic limb control
item.description: Researchers hope to use these sensors to help people with amputation achieve more natural movements with their prosthetic limbs.
item.dc:creator: Anne Trafton | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
MIT researchers have shown that they can accurately track muscle movement using tiny magnetic beads implanted in the muscle. These measurements could make it easier for people with certain types of amputations to control their prosthetic limbs.

For decades, researchers have been working to develop neuroprosthetic limbs, which use neural information from muscles remaining after an amputation to guide the prosthetic limb. Measurements of a muscle’s length, velocity and activation can be fed into the control algorithms that guide the limbs, allowing individuals with leg amputation to walk with a more natural gait, or those with arm amputation to manipulate objects more effectively.

Until now, these devices have relied on muscle activity measurements from electrodes placed on the surface of the skin. However, those measurements have not proven reliable enough to ensure safety while walking with a neuroprosthetic leg. 

The MIT team hopes that their new magnetic tracking system, which offers more accurate measurements, will enable commercial development of such limbs.

“For four decades, the standard methodology for neurally controlling prostheses has been to use skin electrodes to measure muscle activation. However, to control a prosthetic limb, joint position, torque, or impedance has to be controlled, and one cannot directly determine such mechanical signals using electrical activation alone,” says Hugh Herr, a professor of media arts and sciences, co-director of the K. Lisa Yang Center for Bionics at MIT, an associate member of MIT’s McGovern Institute for Brain Research, and the senior author of the new study.

In the new study, which appears today in Nature Sensors, the researchers demonstrated the accuracy of the magnetic measurements in three participants with below-knee amputations.

“This interface is minimally invasive, so it could be accessible to more people. You place two beads in the muscle and you have access to all of this rich information about the muscle dynamics,” says Christopher Shallal, an MIT graduate student in the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology and one of the lead authors of the paper.

The paper’s other lead author is Cameron Taylor PhD ’20, an assistant professor of biomedical engineering at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Tracking muscles

For many years, Herr’s lab has been developing human-machine interfaces that can be used to control an artificial limb in a way that makes it more like using a natural limb. Obtaining accurate measurements of how the user is moving the muscles at the amputation site is critical to the success of this type of prosthesis.

Electrodes on the surface of the skin can reveal the electrical activation of the muscle below, and those measurements can be converted to estimates of how much a muscle is contracting or flexing. Based on that input, a robotic controller generates commands that guide the prosthetic limb in the user’s intended direction. 

However, that measurement approach, known as electromyography, does not always provide accurate enough information. The electrical signal is not a perfect proxy for muscle dynamics; for example, when a muscle is held at a fixed length for several seconds, the signal fades. Additionally, the electrodes may pick up signals from muscles other than the intended target, and sweat can interfere with detection of the signal.

Last year, Herr and his colleagues reported a “bionic knee” prosthesis that uses electrodes implanted in the muscles to provide accurate measurements and feed them into a robotic controller. This approach proved successful in a small clinical study, but alongside that work, Herr’s team has also been working on a less invasive approach that relies on magnets instead of electrodes.

With this approach, known as magnetomicrometry, pairs of magnets are implanted into muscles. When a muscle contracts or stretches, external sensors placed on the skin can measure the change in distance between the magnets, allowing muscle length and velocity to be calculated.

“Magnets can be tracked wirelessly through the body, so you can get very specific muscle signals and measure the mechanical output of the muscle without needing to be extremely invasive,” Shallal says.

Better control

In a 2021 study led by Taylor, Herr’s lab first demonstrated the magnet-based technique in animal models. The new Nature Sensors study extends the approach to humans with long-term magnetic implants. For the study, the researchers recruited three participants who have below-knee amputations.

All of these participants had a type of amputation that creates what’s called an agonist-antagonist myoneural interface (AMI). With this surgical procedure, muscle pairs are reconnected during surgery so that they still dynamically communicate with each other within the residual limb. This sensory feedback, called proprioception, helps the wearer of the prosthesis to decide how to position and move their prosthetic limb. 

Participants had magnets implanted in up to four muscles of the ankle joint. The surgeries were performed at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in collaboration with plastic surgeon Matthew Carty, a co-author of the study. The beads are 3 millimeters in diameter, about the size of a sesame seed. The magnets are made from an alloy of neodymium, iron, and boron, and are coated with gold and a polymer called parylene C to make them biocompatible. The magnetic signals can be read from a depth of up to 6 centimeters from the skin’s surface, using a customized external sensor that is worn over the skin, positioned over the muscles that are being tracked. 

Each of the participants in this study also had electrodes implanted into the same muscles that received magnetic beads. This allowed the researchers to compare the accuracy of three different types of measurements: magnetomicrometry, electromyography with implanted electrodes, and electromyography with electrodes on the surface of the skin.

During the experiments, the participants were not wearing a prosthetic limb but were asked to perform tasks such as moving a cursor on a screen to a particular target using their muscle movements. Using each of the three measurement techniques, the signals generated by the muscle movements were translated into control signals that, in this case, moved the cursor but in the future could be fed into the controller of a robotic ankle-foot prosthesis.  

“The cursor on the screen represented the degrees of freedom that they would control on a robotic ankle-foot prosthesis. This virtual neuroprosthetic task allowed us to compare the performance across different neural interfaces, and our results suggest that the magnet-based approach can offer more accurate and stable control,” Shallal says.

The researchers are now performing a larger study in which they are evaluating how well people can control prosthetic limbs using measurements from the magnetic beads. 

The research was funded, in part, by the Yang Tan Collective at MIT as well as a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship and an MIT HEALS Graduate Fellowship.

item.title: New system gives users more control over their online experience
item.description: The Social.Wiki framework enables anyone to easily edit social websites within the system, while allowing them to choose the content they see.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
A user who is frustrated with changes a social media company made to their favorite messaging platform, like the introduction of an annoying AI chatbot, can’t do much to address the situation, short of leaving the platform.

Now, MIT researchers are offering an alternative path.

They’ve created Social.Wiki, a system that allows users to easily edit any social application made within Social.Wiki, and choose which of the edits made by others they want to see. 

For example, a user could change a messaging site on Social.Wiki to remove an AI chatbot and instead add a restaurant voting feature so their group chat can finally decide where they are going out for dinner.

“The infrastructure that we are all dependent on online is very rigid. It is based on these one-size-fits-all applications that we don’t have a lot of power to change. This project is about trying to imagine what a different web would look like where anyone can participate,” says Theia Henderson, an electrical engineering and computer science (EECS) graduate student, and lead author of a new paper on Social.Wiki.

The researchers envision a world in which, if a user is unhappy with their social app, they can edit it to change it however they like — without getting cut off from their social connections.

The platform enables users with no coding expertise to create a range of websites, including social sites like photo sharing networks, discussion forums, and dating apps. It handles all back-end work, eliminating the need for creators to set up servers or arrange databases.

Social.Wiki employs a decentralized infrastructure that allows users to retain ownership of their data as they create, edit, and navigate social websites within the platform. It also includes a “data guard” that protects user data from malicious or buggy applications. 

Through case studies and user tests, the researchers demonstrated the breadth of applications people can create with Social.Wiki, including a rideshare app where riders propose the prices they are willing to pay and a collaborative canvas for creating art together.

While Social.Wiki is still in its early days, the researchers plan to continue refining the platform as they deploy it to a wider audience. 

“We want to empower the creation of far more social applications that meet the needs of unusual small groups. Each group is unusual, but everyone is in unusual groups. Everybody has their own needs for social applications that we want to be able to address,” says David Karger, professor of EECS, a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), and senior author of the paper.

Henderson and Karger are joined on the paper by EECS graduate students Carmel Schare and Ana Dodik; Clemens Klokmose, a professor of computer science at Aarhus University in Denmark; Ziv Epstein, a postdoc in the MIT Media Lab; and David D. Clark, an MIT research scientist. The paper will be presented at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in November.

Letting users choose

Social.Wiki is a Wikipedia-like system in which users can navigate to different web applications or create their own web application within the Social.Wiki ecosystem. Each website has an “edit” button that allows any user to change the content of the site, from the text color on a message board to the pricing algorithm in a ride-sharing app.

Clicking the “edit” button in Social.Wiki opens a page that lets users view and edit the source code manually or prompt an AI assistant to make changes to the site. 

This platform builds on the researchers’ prior work on Graffiti, a web framework with a decentralized infrastructure that makes building personalized applications easier. 

With Social.Wiki, the researchers sought a collaboratively editable system that would allow anyone to revise web applications to be ideally suited for their needs and the needs of groups they belong to. 

To enable this structure, Social.Wiki relies on a strategy the researchers call “plural governance.” Instead of a central moderator deciding which content users will see, each Social.Wiki user can choose the rules that determine which edits they will see on Social.Wiki webpages.

Users can also identify “trusted editors,” so they will see edits from individuals or organizations they consider reliable.

For instance, a user could customize their rules, or “governance policy,” so they only see edits to a site that have been endorsed by at least two of their friends. When the Social.Wiki browser loads a site for a user, it applies the governance policy that user selected to decide which version of the site to present.

For example, based on each user’s choices and edits, the system might show one user a ride-sharing app with a uniform pricing algorithm while another user might see the same app with a dynamic pricing algorithm.

“No website is tied to a particular machine. This means we have no centralized ownership over the websites or the underlying infrastructure,” Henderson explains.

Security and creativity

In this decentralized infrastructure, user data are stored separately from the websites that access it, which helps keep data secure.

Social.Wiki also employs a data guard, which prompts a user to review each request from a website that is attempting to access their data.

“In Social.Wiki, these websites are held in common and anybody can edit them, but the data guard makes sure that each user stays in control of what happens to their data,” Karger adds.

The researchers evaluated Social.Wiki through several case studies. For one, they developed a messaging platform that allows participants to modify the chat’s styling and interface without affecting the experience of others. In another, they built a collaborative ride-sharing app that enables riders to adjust the fare they want to pay using a transparent “living wage” calculator.

They also sponsored a hackathon in which users built Social.Wiki applications.

Participants developed a range of creative sites, including a housing co-op communication tool that organizes chats on a map of the co-op, as well as a garden-themed microblogging site where posts are “planted” as flowers.

“Even the little bit that has been done so far with Social.Wiki demonstrates that there is so much more that could be done with social apps if users could specialize them to meet a particular group’s needs,” Karger says.

Moving forward, the researchers are working to deploy Social.Wiki to a broader audience and gather feedback from more diverse user groups. They also want to make technical upgrades to enable end-to-end encryption on private message data and provide better developer tools.

This work was funded, in part, by Schmidt Sciences and the National Science Foundation (NSF).

item.title: Capturing the complete process of embryonic development
item.description: By tracking over 1 million cells, researchers created a detailed map of embryonic development in mice. It could provide development and disease insights.
item.dc:creator: Shafaq Zia | Whitehead Institute
item.content:encoded:
For decades, scientists have been able to look at individual moments in the development of an embryo: a snapshot of a developing brain, a picture of how the heart takes shape, or a glimpse of cells beginning to form the nervous system.

But what if instead of taking snapshots, they could watch the entire process unfold?

A new study out of the lab of MIT Professor Jonathan Weissman, a member of the Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and a Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator, offers one of the most detailed views yet of how a mammal is built, cell by cell.

By following the family history of over a million cells as a mouse embryo develops, the researchers have created a kind of developmental blueprint, or movie, showing how cells divide and ultimately become the tissues and organs in the body.

This open-access work, published Oct. 8 in the journal Cell, in collaboration with Zachary Smith’s group at Yale University and the Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics, provides a comprehensive view of a process that has long been studied in pieces: how a single fertilized egg gives rise to hundreds of different kinds of cells, arranged in the right places and at the right times to build an animal.

“This is really a view of how the information in the genome plays out over space and time to go from linear DNA to a three-dimensional animal,” Weissman says.

The map could have broad implications for understanding birth defects and cancer. Many birth defects arise when cells change course as tissues and organs are being assembled. A detailed map of typical development could help researchers pinpoint where and when those processes go awry. In cancer, the same approach could help scientists trace when cells acquire traits such as the ability to spread or resist treatment. 

The map could also inform stem cell research by revealing the sequence of cell states that leads to mature, functional cell types.

In the 1980s, scientists ventured into similar territory by painstakingly following the development of Caenorhabditis elegans, a tiny worm whose transparent body contains only about 1,000 cells. Using microscopy, they could trace how individual cells divided and where their descendants ended up.

But achieving something similar in a mammal was a challenge on a vastly different scale. Mammalian embryos contain far more cells, develop inside the uterus — out of sight — and do not follow a completely predetermined script.

The new study tackles this challenge using a technology developed in the Weissman Lab called PEtracer. The system acts somewhat like a flight recorder inside a cell. PEtracer makes small, heritable changes to DNA that are passed down as cells divide. By reading those changes later, scientists can work backward to reconstruct which cells came from which ancestors, essentially building a family tree for the cells in the developing embryo.

In this work, the researchers combined these family trees with information about what genes were turned on in each cell and where these cells were located in the embryo. They analyzed over a million cells from mouse embryos collected at multiple points during development, allowing them to follow not just where cells ended up, but when they began heading toward particular fates.

A new study from Jay Shendure’s group at the University of Washington, published concurrently in the journal Science, uses a related approach called DNA Typewriter to track cell divisions in developing mouse embryos and build a record of their cellular history. 

Both studies provide a much more comprehensive look at mammalian development than existed previously. The Weissman team, however, studied embryos at closely spaced stages of development, looking at multiple embryos at each stage. This gave them a more detailed picture of how development unfolds and allowed them to ask how consistently cells follow the same paths from one embryo to another. 

With this detailed timeline, the researchers could also determine when cells commit to particular fates, how many early cells go on to form a tissue, and how they ultimately contribute to the developing organ.

While earlier studies might focus on one cell population, this approach puts those individual stories into the context of the entire developing animal — a perspective that is particularly useful for understanding disease. 

Cancer, for example, is not a single event, but a process in which cells acquire new characteristics over time, including the ability to spread or resist treatment. A lineage map could allow researchers to trace when those characteristics emerge and how cells change as they acquire them.

“Development and cancer both depend on decisions cells make about what they will become,” says Luke Koblan, a postdoc in the Weissman Lab and co-first author of the paper. “By tracing how cells develop in mouse embryos, we hope to better understand how cancer cells change in ways that help them spread or resist treatment.”

The work could also provide a new guide for stem cell research. Scientists have spent decades trying to coax stem cells into becoming mature, functional versions of particular cell types for research or potential therapies. But reproducing the precise conditions in an embryo is difficult.

“If we could have a step-by-step recipe for how to create every cell type in the body,” says graduate student and co-first author William Colgan, “that would be incredibly powerful for stem cell biology.”

Weissman compares the work to the Human Genome Project: knowing the sequence of the human genome gave scientists the ingredients — but not the instructions for how those ingredients are used — to build an organism.

“The genome is like the ingredient list for a four-course meal,” he says. “It tells you what the ingredients are, but it doesn’t tell you which ones you use when, how much you use, or where you put them. Without the recipe, it’s impossible to know how those ingredients can become the meal.”

This new map begins to fill in the details of that missing recipe. The result is a resource that researchers can use to explore mammalian development in a fundamentally new way. Rather than studying development as a collection of separate processes, scientists can now begin to see how those processes fit together into one unfolding story.

item.title: How the biggest Alzheimer’s risk gene disrupts the process of insulating neurons
item.description: MIT researchers showed that the APOE4 gene variant suppresses molecular signaling needed for oligodendrocytes to myelinate neurons and also demonstrated a proof-of-concept fix.
item.dc:creator: David Orenstein | The Picower Institute for Learning and Memory
item.content:encoded:
One of the main ways that the APOE4 gene variant, the biggest genetic risk factor for late onset Alzheimer’s disease, undermines brain circuit function is by disrupting the process of insulating neurons with a fatty sheath that optimizes their electrical transmission. A new study led by neuroscientists at the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory at MIT provides several lines of evidence to implicate a specific molecular pathway in that disruption, and uses that insight to demonstrate an intervention for preventing it in lab experiments.

The study, published Oct. 15 in Cell Stem Cell, shows that APOE4 leads to a suppression of “Wnt” signaling in the oligodendrocyte cells that provide neurons with a fatty insulation, called myelin. When Wnt signaling is deficient, they showed, the cells accumulate droplets of lipids rather than deploying fats to properly myelinate the neurons’ axon branches. When the researchers restored Wnt signaling in APOE4-carrying oligodendrocytes, myelination rebounded, both in human cell cultures and in mice modeling Alzheimer’s.

The research team, led by Picower Professor Li-Huei Tsai and study lead author Leyla Akay PhD ’25, a former graduate student in Tsai’s lab, discovered Wnt’s key role via multiple methods, including a screen in which they used CRISPR gene editing to systematically knock out each protein-coding gene in the genome, one by one, in cultures of human APOE4-carrying oligodendrocytes. The screen showed that when genes promoting Wnt activity in oligodendrocytes were lacking, lipid droplets accumulated, and that when genes suppressing Wnt were lacking, lipid droplets were, too.

“This proof of principle of doing CRISPR screens for genetic modifiers of APOE4-associated lipid accumulation in a central nervous system cell type is very exciting,” says Tsai, who also directs MIT’s Aging Brain Initiative. “I think this type of screen not only provides new insights into cellular pathways contributing to lipid metabolism defects, but really also has the potential to provide new targets for drug development.”

For want of Wnt

In 2022, Tsai’s Lab, led by Akay, Djuna Von Maydell PhD ’25, Jose Davila-Velderrain, and Joel Blanchard (also a co-author of the new study), showed that APOE4 caused lipid droplet accumulation in oligodendrocytes and upset myelination. But, Akay says, that droplet accumulation could happen for many reasons. The new study sought to dig deeper into the underlying molecular mechanisms.

“This CRISPR screen allowed us an unbiased way to test every single possibility,” Akay says. “What kind of lipid enzymes are involved in this process? And what are upstream pathways that could be targeted?”

In parallel with the CRISPR screen, the team also analyzed the chromatin accessibility of the DNA in human oligodendrocyte cell cultures and in postmortem human brain samples, in each case comparing APOE4-carrying samples to ones carrying the neutral APOE3 variant. This analysis of ATAC-seq data allowed them to assess which genes were most accessible for expression versus which ones were locked down from transcription. The chromatin analysis showed that genes promoting Wnt signaling were less accessible in APOE4 carriers.

“There was a striking overlap between ATAC-seq and CRISPR screen results,” Tsai says. “Both pointed to a dysregulation of the Wnt signaling pathway.” 

Toward a therapy

Further analysis, including direct observations in cells at the lab bench, revealed how Wnt signaling became depressed in cultured APOE4 oligodendrocytes. Two proteins, beta-catenin and GSK3b, each compete to regulate Wnt — beta-catenin promotes it, and GSK3b suppresses it. The team found that in APOE4 oligodendrocytes compared to APOE3 ones, there was reduced beta-catenin expression and excessive GSK3b expression.

The team then tested interventions that manipulate GSK3b activity. In human APOE3 oligodendrocyte cultures, they showed that increasing GSK3b with a chemical called Dif3 increased lipid droplets. In APOE4 oligodendrocytes, they showed that inhibiting GSK3b with a chemical called CHIR99021 reduced droplets. In more complex “organoid” cultures combining APOE4 oligodendrocytes with neurons, they found that inhibiting GSK3b increased myelination and promoted the growth of neural axons.

The tests suggested that GSK3b inhibition could be a proof-of-concept therapeutic strategy for restoring Wnt signaling and myelination. As a final test, they treated mice carrying APOE4 and genetically modeling Alzheimer’s tau pathology with doses of CHIR99021. The treated mice exhibited a reduction in lipid droplets in the hippocampus of the brain, a key memory-making region. Moreover, they also showed increased myelination there, compared to untreated controls.

In addition to highlighting suppression of Wnt signaling, the CRISPR screen and chromatin analysis provided key clues about the molecular mechanisms by which loss of Wnt alters how oligodendrocytes metabolize lipids. Akay and Tsai say they are eager to follow up on those clues. They are also interested in investigating GSK3b’s linkage to tau phosphorylation, a major feature of Alzheimer’s pathology.

In addition to Tsai, Akay, and Blanchard, the paper’s other authors are Anna Bright, Daiyun Dong, Ethan Smith, Robert Hurt, Carles Boix, Kate Louderback, Janine Medrano, Dingcheng Sun, Haonan Lin, Oisín King, Gwyneth Welch, Hiba Nawaid, Emre Agbas, Alan Jiang, Adele Bubnys, and Ji-Xin Cheng.

The National Institutes of Health, the Robert and Renee E. Belfer Family Foundation, the Manthripragada McManama Alzheimer's Fund, the CAMA Seed Fund, the J. Crayton Pruitt Foundation, Joseph P. DiSabato and Nancy Sakamoto, and the Freedom Together Foundation provided funding for the study.

Raw data from the study is available on the Open Science Framework. Akay and Tsai have applied for a patent on the CRISPR screen results.

item.title: A soft robot could help doctors diagnose and treat disorders of the small intestine
item.description: MIT engineers designed a robotic enteroscope that can inch through the hard-to-reach small intestine, making biopsies and drug delivery easier.
item.dc:creator: Anne Trafton | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
Disorders of the small intestine are often difficult to diagnose and treat. More than 20 feet long, an inch in diameter, and located deep within the body, this organ is harder to access than other parts of the digestive tract, such as the colon or stomach.

To overcome those challenges, MIT engineers have designed a new robotic enteroscope that can move easily through the narrow passage of the small intestine, allowing it to perform imaging, deliver drugs, and remove small polyps or tissue samples for biopsy.

In designing the new robot, the researchers were inspired by the locomotion of snakes, as well as the scaly skin that helps them gain traction on slippery surfaces. A special textured coating helps the robot remain attached to the mucosal lining of the intestine as it inches its way through the narrow tube. 

Similar to an endoscope, the robot contains a variety of tools to help detect and treat any abnormalities that it might encounter.

“When we evaluate the small intestine, we do it for either diagnosis or treatment. If we find a little polyp that needs to be removed, this robot allows us to take a biopsy or remove it,” says Giovanni Traverso, professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, a gastroenterologist at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, and an associate member of the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.

Traverso is the senior author of the study, which appears today in Science Robotics. The paper’s lead authors are former MIT postdoc Binbin Ying, who is now an assistant professor at University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center; MIT graduate student Ahmad Mujtaba Jebran; and former MIT research scientist Sahab Babaee.

Snaking through the intestine

The most common problems that doctors need to evaluate within the small intestine include bleeding, lesions, and blockages.

Currently, the only way to diagnose those intestinal complications is with a procedure known as double balloon enteroscopy. During the procedure, an enteroscope advances through the small intestine as a health care worker alternately inflates and deflates two balloons that help propel it through the tract. 

This process is slow and laborious, so the MIT team wanted to design an alternative enteroscope that would be easier to control and could move faster through the intestine.

“The fundamental challenge that we’re trying to overcome is how to evaluate that 20-to-25-foot segment of the small intestine in a way that can be more automated,” Traverso says.

The new tube-like robot moves through the narrow small intestine using a locomotion strategy similar to that of the snake. When slithering along the ground, a snake can steer itself by first contracting muscles on one side of the body, then the other. 

To mimic this, the researchers designed multifunctional actuators that control the robot’s movement. Each actuator contains four chambers, which can be inflated in different combinations, prompting the tube to extend or bend in any direction. 

“By tuning the amount of air that goes into these chambers, you can tune the direction that the robot is moving in,” Traverso says.

The head and tail segments of the robot contain additional expandable anchoring balloons that take turns inflating and deflating, helping the robot move forward. These head and tail segments are coated with special patterned sleeves inspired by kirigami — a variation of origami that involves cutting paper as well as folding it.

Using this technique, the researchers created coatings that lie flat until they are stretched by the expansion of the balloon, which causes three-dimensional kirigami needles to pop out. Similar to the scales of a snake, these needles give the robot more traction within the slippery lining of the intestine. 

In previous work, Traverso’s lab has used this approach to create coatings for shoe soles that give them more traction, as well as stents that can temporarily lodge in the esophagus and release drugs. 

“By using kirigami sleeves to enhance surface friction, the robot can generate localized tissue engagement traction for locomotion without relying on excessive stretching of the delicate small intestinal tissue,” Jebran says.

Diagnosis and treatment

The system also includes electronics that allow for navigation, with a controller that the person operating the device can use to guide the robot through narrow passages and around tight corners. The soft robot is tethered to the external controllers by a cable and is designed so that it could enter the body through either the mouth or the rectum. 

The robot contains tools including a camera for imaging, a sprayer for drug delivery, and clips that can take tissue biopsies or remove polyps. 

In animal studies, the researchers showed that the robot could travel about six and a half feet through the small intestine. They also successfully demonstrated the drug sprayer, tissue clips, and camera. The team is now working on improving the navigation systems and testing this approach for additional applications in the small intestine.

“We hope we can continue to move it forward to eventually develop systems that can help achieve more automated evaluation of the small intestine,” Traverso says.

The research was funded, in part, by the Karl van Tassel Career Development Professorship, the MIT Department of Mechanical Engineering, a Banting Postdoctoral Fellowship, an NSERC Postdoctoral Fellowship, the UT Southwestern Medical Center Startup Fund, Samsung Semiconductor and Eurnekian Nanotechnology Graduate Student Fellowships, the Cooke Undergraduate Transfer Scholarship, and the MIT Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program.

item.title: Origami-based construction method yields lightweight, load-bearing structures on architectural scales
item.description: The modular approach could be used to erect emergency shelters or fabricate aerospace components more quickly and with less material than some techniques.
item.dc:creator: Adam Zewe | MIT News
item.content:encoded:
MIT researchers developed a new type of origami-based construction method that could be used to build complex structures that are cheaper and easier to assemble, and use less material than those built with some conventional techniques.

This scalable system simplifies the process of designing lightweight, rigid structural shells from modular components that can be fabricated from flat sheets of material and then folded into shape. 

The units are connected to build a larger lattice structure using simple tools and a foolproof assembly process. They form a strong, load-bearing structural shell that doesn’t need interior support columns.

This method could be particularly well-suited for disaster relief shelters that can be rapidly fabricated and shipped efficiently as flat panels, then set up quickly by workers at the site of an earthquake or flood. It could also be used to develop strong, lightweight components for airplanes or modular robots, or architectural elements like sound-dampening panels and building facades.

The researchers’ technique can generate structures that are many times stiffer than those made using some other forms of structural origami, while requiring only about two-thirds as much material. This could make it a more sustainable form of construction.

In addition to developing small prototypes, the researchers demonstrated the scalability of this approach by fabricating a room-sized folded aluminum sculpture that was recently hung at the Boston Public Library as an exhibition inaugurated for the annual Fab Lab Conference and Symposium.

“This work shows that the power of digital manufacturing can go beyond personal fabrication projects and start touching the real world, enhancing the way we design houses and large structures. We are demonstrating structural origami on building scales,” says Alfonso Parra Rubio, a graduate student in the Center for Bits and Atoms (CBA) at MIT and lead author of a paper on this method.

He is joined on the paper by Riccardo Foschi, a researcher at the University of Bologna in Italy; Rupert Maleczek, a senior scientist at the University of Innsbruck in Austria; Tomohiro Tachi, a professor at the University of Tokyo; and senior author Neil Gershenfeld, an MIT professor and the director of the CBA. The research appears in the International Journal of Solids and Structures.

Lightweight, rigid components

The researchers drew inspiration from the folded tessellations developed by the artist and scientist Ron Resch in the 1960s. Resch employed repeating patterns of polygonal unit cells to create complex 3D structures (like a honeycomb). 

But rather than creating a shape from one folded piece of material, like Resch’s tessellations, the researchers fabricate unit cells that are folded individually and connected to form the 3D structure.

By designing individual building blocks, they can simplify the fabrication process and create more complex shapes.

While working in the Tachi lab, Parra Rubio developed a method for combining two tripod-shaped unit cells from a Resch tessellation into a building block that has zero degrees of freedom, which means it is completely rigid and locked in place. 

These rigid building blocks can be connected into a network of interwoven beams that form a 3D structure with extremely high stiffness and stability, but very light weight.

“This helps us build strong structures while minimizing the amount of material we are using,” Parra Rubio explains.

But it would be enormously challenging to manually design polygonal building blocks that will form a structure that meets a user’s constraints.

To simplify the process, Parra Rubio joined forces with CBA graduate student Erik Strand to develop an automated solver that designs a series of manufacturable unit cells that will form the user’s desired structure. These design files can be fed to a CNC milling machine that automatically cuts the building blocks from flat sheets of material, like aluminum. 

“On the computational part, we break this big problem down into many small subproblems. Now, we solve each cell independently to make sure that it is foldable, and then we globally assemble them after that,” Strand says.

Simplified assembly

Builders fold the individual units into shape and assemble them into a finished structure using only hand tools, like screwdrivers. 

The assembly process does not require any large-scale welding equipment, which could make it simpler, faster, and cheaper than some other forms of construction. In addition, the unit cells are designed so they adjust naturally into their correct shape as the structure is assembled. 

“The way the unit cells are designed, the structure can only exist in one configuration. The connection is the same everywhere, even though each unit cell is different,” Parra Rubio says.

Simulations indicated that this method yields structures about 3.5 times stiffer than those made with some other origami-based techniques, while using less material. In addition, the resulting structures could be strong enough for some architectural applications, Parra Rubio adds. 

To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, the researchers assembled a 23-foot sculpture from pieces of folded aluminum that was hung from the ceiling of the atrium in the Boston Public Library. A team with no professional construction experience built the entire structure in a matter of days, Parra Rubio says.

“It was really fun to work on something at such a quick pace where the theory was really meeting a practical use for it. We had to think a lot about how we could tweak the design to achieve each objective,” Strand says.

In the future, the researchers want to test this approach in larger, architectural structures. They also want to explore the use of unit cells with more complex geometries, which could offer greater strength or stiffness, and develop a user-friendly design interface. 

“This work shows that folding metal is a method that is ready to be used for building structures. We can do it big enough and strong enough, now that we can bring it out of the lab and to the construction site,” Gershenfeld says.

“Within the architecture, engineering, and construction industry, complex structures are often delivered through a fragmented sequence of handoffs between design, engineering, fabrication, and construction teams, with each transition creating opportunities for miscoordination, rework, and loss of design intent. By embedding geometric, structural performance, and assembly intelligence directly into each module, Rubio’s approach maintains a seamless digital thread from design through erection, enabling unprecedented customization while ensuring precise execution,” says James Coleman, SM ’14, MArch ’14, cofounder of SumPoint, a project installation specialty firm. 

Coleman, the former Vice President of R&D at A. Zahner Company, was not involved with this research. His recent work on the design, fabrication, and erection of complex architectural projects includes the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, Air Force Academy Cadet Chapel, Google Headquarters, and SoFi Stadium.

This research was funded, in part, by the Center for Bits and Atoms Research Consortia, the University of Bologna in Italy, and the Austrian Research Agency.
